opus-5.5.text:
That period was really formative for me. With MoCo v3, the goal was pretty simple at first: take contrastive learning, which worked well with ConvNets, and move it to Vision Transformers. But the most interesting thing we found wasn't the final number. It was that training was surprisingly unstable. You'd see these dips in the training curve where accuracy suddenly dropped and then recovered, and it didn't always show up as a catastrophic failure. It could quietly hurt your results. We found tricks, like freezing the patch projection layer, that made it more stable. But the bigger lesson for me was that a lot of what we thought were "method" improvements were really about optimization and the recipe, and that when you scale up, those hidden issues become the dominant factor.

Then masked autoencoders felt almost like a counterpoint. MAE was very simple: mask out a large fraction of the patches, like 75%, and reconstruct the pixels. No negative pairs, no heavy augmentation engineering. And it scaled quite gracefully with model size, and it was efficient because the encoder only sees the visible patches. That simplicity mattered a lot. It made me believe the vision community had overcomplicated things, and that the right formulation can make scaling much easier.

But honestly, both experiences also left me with some unease. In language, self-supervised learning, basically next-token prediction, became the whole story. You scale it and you get general capabilities. In vision, even with MoCo v3 and MAE, we were still mostly evaluating on ImageNet fine-tuning or linear probing. We were scaling models, but we weren't really scaling data in the same way, and we weren't asking whether these representations were useful for broader things like multimodal understanding. So the gap between "this works on ImageNet" and "this is a foundation for intelligence" was still very large.

That's why later I became interested in revisiting the question more directly: if you really scale visual self-supervised learning on large and diverse data, not curated ImageNet, can it compete with language-supervised models like CLIP? And I think the answer is more optimistic than people assumed. A lot of the perceived ceiling came from the setup, not from the idea of learning from pixels alone.

So my overall view is that self-supervised learning in vision is not a solved problem and not a dead end. The lesson from MoCo v3 is that stability and recipes matter enormously at scale. The lesson from MAE is that simplicity scales. And the remaining lesson, which I'm still working on, is that we need to scale the data and rethink the evaluation, so that we measure whether vision models actually understand the world, not just whether they classify ImageNet well.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Those two projects really were formative, and in some ways they taught me opposite lessons that ended up fitting together.

With MoCo V3, we were trying to answer a fairly simple question: can contrastive learning, which had worked so well for ConvNets, just transfer to Vision Transformers? And the honest answer was, sort of, but it was fragile. We spent a lot of time chasing training instabilities. The loss would look fine, and then you'd see these sudden dips in accuracy, and we traced it back to things like the patch embedding layer, where gradients would spike. We ended up freezing it, which is kind of an embarrassing fix when you think about it. But that experience made me skeptical of the idea that you could just take a recipe designed around one architecture and one data regime and crank up the dial. The method was leaning heavily on augmentations, on carefully balanced negatives, on tricks that encoded a lot of human priors about what invariances matter. And every one of those priors is a potential bottleneck when you scale.

Then MAE came along, and it was almost the opposite philosophy. Mask most of the image, reconstruct the pixels, done. No contrastive pairs, no momentum encoder, no augmentation beyond a random crop. What struck me was how little it needed. The pretext task was so simple that it almost felt like it shouldn't work, and yet it scaled cleanly to the largest models we could train at the time, and it was far more efficient because you only encode the visible patches. The thing I took away was that in vision, the hard part isn't designing a clever objective. It's removing the inductive biases that stop the model from learning on its own as you add data and compute.

So putting those together, my view became that scaling self-supervised learning is less about the loss function and more about what you take out. Language had this nice property where next-token prediction is a natural, dense, scalable signal. Vision doesn't have an obvious equivalent, and I think a lot of the field's work, including mine, has been a search for that. MAE got close in spirit, but reconstruction in pixel space still has limits. Pixels are a noisy target, and a lot of what you learn is low-level. That's actually part of why I've since gravitated toward thinking about the representation itself as the target, and toward questions like what happens when you connect these visual encoders to language models. The lesson from MoCo V3 and MAE was really: trust the data, trust the scale, and be very suspicious of your own cleverness.

astra-6.text:
Working on MoCo V3 and masked autoencoders made me think about scaling as more than simply making a model bigger. You need an objective and a training recipe that let the model actually benefit from that extra capacity.

With MoCo V3, we were exploring contrastive learning with vision transformers, and training stability became an important part of the story. It’s easy to look at a result and conclude that an architecture doesn’t work well, when the limitation may actually be in how you optimize it. That made me more careful about separating those two things.

Masked autoencoders offered a different perspective. You hide a large portion of an image and ask the model to reconstruct what’s missing. It’s a simple task, but it creates a useful learning problem without requiring human labels. And because the encoder processes only the visible patches, you can spend your computation more efficiently.

So the lesson for me was that simplicity and scalability can reinforce each other. The question isn’t just whether a method gets a better number at one model size. It’s whether, as you give it more data and more compute, it continues to learn useful representations—and whether the cost makes that scaling practical.

sol-6.1.text:
Those two projects made me think about scaling as more than making the model bigger. You also have to ask whether the learning objective and the training procedure let you benefit from that scale.

With MoCo V3, we were exploring contrastive learning with vision transformers. A lot of the work was about understanding optimization and stability. That experience taught me to be careful when interpreting results: if a larger model doesn’t improve, is that a limitation of the representation, or have we simply failed to train it well?

Masked autoencoders offered a different perspective. You hide a large portion of the image and ask the model to reconstruct it. Because the encoder only processes visible patches, you can train a large encoder quite efficiently. So the objective and the architecture work together to make scaling practical.

For me, the broader lesson was that simplicity can be very powerful. But a simple idea still requires careful design. What matters is finding a learning problem that gets useful supervision from the data and continues to improve as you give it more capacity and computation.
